title: Former Car Dealer Exposes 10 Warranty Tricks Dealerships Desperately Hope You Never Discover
summary: A self-described former 6-year F&I employee details ten sales tricks dealerships use to sell extended warranties, from payment packing to pre-existing-condition claim denials and a hard-to-use cancellation process.

assertions.quote: makes between 1200 and 1800 every time they sell you an extended warranty. The warranty company that actually pays the claims, they keep about 400.

verdicts.note: Plausible given known F&I markup practices, but is one insider's self-reported figure rather than a verified industry average, and markups vary widely.

WTAMU (citing J.D. Power 2001) found dealers earned an average profit of $548 on a service-contract retail price of $1,178 -- directionally consistent with the dealer capturing most of the profit, but well below the $1,200-$1,800 range the claim states.

assertions.quote: This is called packing the payment. It means they show you one monthly number that includes the car, the warranty, gap insurance, tire and wheel

verdicts.note: A widely documented F&I sales practice known as 'payment packing.'
A well-documented pricing-framing effect used broadly in sales, including for warranty products.

assertions.quote: I could buy a warranty from the warranty company for $1,800 and sell it to you for $3,200

verdicts.note: Consistent with markup practices described by multiple insiders, though the specific dollar figures are one narrator's example, not a verified average.

NCLC: pricing of add-ons "is not transparent: generally only the dealer, the finance company, and the third-party add-on provider know what other consumers are paying," alongside dealer markups on service contracts averaging 83% over cost.

assertions.quote: It says if the failure was caused by something that existed before you bought the warranty, the claim is denied
The company that sold you the warranty and the company that pays the claims are often not the same company

verdicts.note: The seller/underwriter/administrator separation is real and documented, but the denial-incentive framing describes a structural incentive, not proof of deliberate denial strategy.

FTC confirms many dealer-sold service contracts are "handled by independent companies called administrators" that "make the decisions about authorizing the payment of claims," distinct from the seller -- but the guide doesn't show that denying more claims increases that administrator's profit.

assertions.quote: electronic components not essential to vehicle operation. That includes the radio. It also includes your backup camera, your Bluetooth system, your navigation

verdicts.note: Broad exclusion language is a commonly cited consumer complaint about vehicle service contracts.

assertions.quote: Most warranties are cancelable. If you don't like it, you can cancel it anytime and get a pro-rated refund. Technically true, practically difficult.
it goes toward your principal, not your pocket
You can't add it later. Not really. Some warranty companies will let you buy coverage after the sale, but it requires a vehicle inspection.

verdicts.note: Consistent with how post-sale vehicle service contract eligibility generally works, though rules vary by provider.

assertions.quote: if you're buying a 3-year-old Toyota with 30,000 miles, you're paying for something you're almost certainly never going to use

verdicts.note: Consistent with how repair-cost and failure-rate risk actually varies by vehicle type, age, and mileage.
